messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Linh's Story

Linh was thirty-eight when the accident happened at the studio where she'd worked for nearly a decade. She'd built her reputation carefully—a master of traditional Vietnamese designs, intricate mandalas, and the kind of fine linework that required absolute steadiness and focus. The studio was her sanctuary, a place where she controlled every variable: the lighting, the music, the pace of her clients' breathing as she worked. On a Tuesday afternoon in late September, a contractor had been refinishing the floor in the back room where supplies were stored, using a industrial-strength chemical stripper that had never been used in the studio before. No one had properly ventilated the space. Linh was mixing pigments when the fumes began to creep through the doorway—a sharp, acrid smell that burned her throat and made her eyes water. By the time she realized something was wrong, the chemical had already entered her lungs. The contractor was shouting, other staff were moving toward the door, but Linh felt frozen, unable to leave her station, unable to move fast enough. She collapsed in the back room, and the last thing she remembered clearly was the taste of metal in her mouth and the feeling of losing control of her own body as it seized.

The hospital stay lasted five days. She was treated for acute chemical pneumonitis, kept on oxygen, monitored constantly. Linh remembered the antiseptic smell of the ward—that clinical, medicinal odor that seemed to coat everything, her skin, her hair, her clothes. She remembered the nurses coming in at all hours, checking her vitals, asking her to describe her symptoms, deciding when she could eat, when she could move, when she could leave. She had no say in any of it. Her body was something to be managed by others. Even as her lungs began to clear and the doctors assured her she would make a full recovery, something had shifted in her. The thought of returning to the studio terrified her. Not because of the work itself, but because of what had happened when she couldn't control the situation. Six months later, Linh tried to go back. She lasted two weeks before she quit entirely.

Now, at forty-four, Linh had been out of tattooing for nearly six years. She worked part-time at a bookstore, shelving inventory, processing returns—work that was solitary and predictable. Her husband, Minh, had been patient, but she could feel the strain. They'd had to downsize their house. The medical bills from the hospitalization had been significant, and her income had never recovered. What frightened Linh most was the thought of being trapped again, of losing control of her circumstances. When she'd tried to return to the studio that second time, she'd found herself hypervigilant to every smell, every change in air quality. A client had come in wearing strong cologne, and Linh had felt her chest tighten, her breathing become shallow. She'd excused herself to the bathroom and hadn't come back.

The triggers were specific and terrifying. If Minh asked her to do something she hadn't planned—to go to dinner with his colleagues, to attend a family gathering—she felt a surge of panic. Being asked to do something meant losing her ability to prepare, to control the environment, to know exactly what would happen and when. At the bookstore, she'd requested that she always work alone in the back room, away from customers and colleagues. When the store manager had suggested she cross-train at the register to be more flexible with scheduling, Linh had felt a familiar dread: the sense of being forced into a situation she hadn't chosen. She'd declined, and the manager had seemed frustrated. The hospital smell haunted her in unexpected moments. Last month, when she'd had to pick up a prescription, the pharmacy's odor—that same chemical-antiseptic blend—had sent her into a panic so severe that she'd left without the medication and sat in her car for an hour.

She'd come to believe that her body was fragile, unreliable, and that the world outside her careful routines was dangerous. Minh had suggested therapy six months ago, but she'd resisted. Now, at her husband's insistence and her own growing despair at how small her life had become, Linh had finally called a therapist. She was terrified that treatment would mean being forced to confront the very things she'd spent six years avoiding, but she was also exhausted by the prison she'd built. She wanted her life back. She wanted to tattoo again. She wanted to feel like she had choices.
